references.text: Expands on the law regarding taking clothing as collateral and specifies that the cloak must be returned before sunset so the poor can sleep in it.
Prohibits taking a widow's clothing as collateral and shows care for vulnerable groups in society.
Job is accused of having taken clothes as collateral without cause and leaving the naked without clothing.
Describes the wicked who take the widow's ox as collateral and drive away the fatherless person's donkey.
The wicked tear the child from the mother's breast and take the poor as collateral.
Warns against taking clothing as collateral from someone who has gone surety for a stranger.
The righteous one returns the pledge to the debtor, as a sign of a righteous way of life.
The wicked withhold the pledge, contrary to God's command.
Israel is accused of lying down beside every altar on clothes taken as collateral.
Deuteronomy expands on the law in Exodus by adding the theological rationale and the consequence of obeying the law of pledges.
Jesus uses the cloak motif from the Exodus law to illustrate a radical ethics that goes beyond the law's demands for justice.
Luke repeats Jesus' teaching about giving up one's cloak, creating a theological contrast between the righteousness of the law and the radicalism of the gospel.
